title: MoD withheld information about nuclear test veterans' records, ex-minister claims
description: Former veterans minister Tobias Ellwood has said the Ministry of Defence (MoD) deliberately withheld information about the medical records of Cold War
body: Former veterans minister Tobias Ellwood has said the Ministry of Defence (MoD) deliberately withheld information about the medical records of Cold War veterans who oversaw nuclear tests.Ellwood told BBC Newsnight he now believes some information he gave to Parliament about the UK's nuclear programme, based on MoD briefings, was "a complete lie".Veterans have campaigned for the release of their medical histories, arguing blood and urine test results could help them prove that nuclear exposure damaged their health.An MoD spokesperson said the government had conducted an "extensive records discovery exercise" to address questions about the programme, with its findings published in full.As many as 25,000 members of the UK armed services, scientists and civilians took part in the nuclear testing programme between 1952 and 1967 at sites including Australia and several islands in the Pacific Ocean.Veterans have claimed the tests caused severe lifelong health problems, alleging they have suffered cancers of the liver, bone, bowel, skin and brain, as well as leukaemia, heart disease, stillbirths and generational birth defects as a result of their exposure.Ellwood, who served as a junior defence minister between June 2017 and July 2019, says he believes ministers over the years have been briefed to say they had no evidence to help nuclear test veterans, as part of an effort to delay until they have passed away.He said the ministry "deliberately withheld" information about the testing programme."The more you unpick this story, the more murky, the more shady, the concerning it becomes," Ellwood told Newsnight. The MoD in 2024 promised to embark on a comprehensive examination of any information the department holds on the issue, and has since released five reports.In those, it said there were a number of factors affecting the way medical records were kept, including the lack of a centralised approach and high levels of Cold War "secrecy". An MoD spokesperson said the government had examined "tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme". They said it had been published in its entirety "following regular engagement between Ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.""We owe an enduring debt of gratitude to the more than 22,000 Service personnel, scientists and civilians who contributed to the UK's nuclear testing programme and helped safeguard our national security," the spokesperson said.

schema.headline: MoD withheld information about nuclear test veterans' records, ex-minister claims

title: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West
description: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in
body: Russian President Vladimir Putin responded with one short sentence when asked at a press conference whether Moscow might strike military facilities in the UK in response to British arms supplies to Ukraine."That's a secret. A military secret."Military secret is not a "yes". And not a "no". It leaves us hanging.And that, I suspect, is the point.Those two words feel like psychological pressure from the Kremlin: to keep Britain guessing - and stressing - over Moscow's intentions, as well as to encourage the UK to think twice about its staunch support for Ukraine.It reminds me of a newspaper article I read a few days ago. Moskovsky Komsomolets had suggested that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham should be seeing Russia, not in his dreams, "but in his nightmares".Scary language. But short on detail about what those nightmares will look like.We cannot conclude that Russian missiles are about to be used against targets in the UK.But look what's happening elsewhere in Europe. Germany now says Russia was responsible for last month's drone attack at Leipzig airport. Putin accused Germany of "planting the evidence". But German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described "the well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe".Could such "operations" now be stepped up in the UK?Yet it wasn't just Britain that received veiled threats at Putin's press conference.So did the West in general. Putin referred to Western countries as sharks."If anyone tries to drag us down the food chain, to gobble us up or devour us, they might get punched in the teeth," he said. "Russia is ready to do that, despite the rapidly growing appetites and teeth of these sharks."Increasingly Russia's president is mixing the geopolitical with the zoological. He recently spoke about killer whales "tearing polar bears apart" to justify Russia's war on Ukraine.The press conference in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, was a fascinating window on Putin's state of mind.For forty-five minutes he took questions from Russian journalists and came across as combative, confident of victory and energised. These days Putin appears most animated when talking about the geopolitical standoff between Russia and the West and the war in Ukraine. Even though the war has not gone to plan. Russia has suffered huge losses on the battlefield and the country's economy is under considerable pressure."I have no doubt that the enemy will crumble," he declared. Yet the war has lasted more than four-and-a-half years and Ukraine fights on.Officially the Kremlin still calls this a "special military operation". But even Putin now is using the word "war"."War is a brutal and unpredictable thing," he said at the press conference.He claimed that he remained open to negotiations to end the conflict and left no doubt with whom he'd prefer to sit down with from the US administration: Donald Trump's envoys."We are absolutely comfortable working with those people we know well and generally trust," Putin said. "[Jared] Kushner and [Steve] Witkoff are always welcome guests. It's a pleasure working with them."There was no such name check for the CIA director who had made a surprise visit to Moscow last week. The Kremlin says the Russian president didn't meet John Ratcliffe during that trip.Is Putin likely to meet Witkoff and Kushner anytime soon?There's nothing in the diary. Not yet.But if they do head to Moscow, President Trump's envoys will encounter a Kremlin leader who remains determined that any peace in Ukraine should be on Russia's terms.

schema.headline: Rosenberg: Putin's veiled threat to UK part of Russia's campaign against West

title: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says
description: Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immedia
body: Andy Burnham's government is "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors" in UK politics, a minister has said in response to calls for an immediate cap on donations.Florence Eshalomi said a new team would be "working at pace to find a solution", as some MPs expressed concerns over the influence of wealthy individuals donating large sums of money.The Labour government has already committed to a £100,000 annual cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, but ministers have been pressed to go further by introducing a limit for UK-based donors.Reform UK's Danny Kruger warned the Representation of the People Bill was a "flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap" the party.Reform has been critical of measures contained in the bill and the impact they could have on funding the party receives from donors.There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties and politicians.Labour MP Stella Creasy said donations from individuals and companies giving £1m or more had "surged" in the last decade and gave examples for different political parties.Among those she named was British billionaire Christopher Harborne, a Thailand-based businessman, who is one of Reform's biggest backers. Last year he gave a single donation of £9m to Reform - the biggest single donation to a UK political party by a living person.Creasy was among those who tabled amendments seeking to also impose a cap on UK-based donors.One of her proposals called for an immediate £500,000 limit which would reduce to £100,000 in the second calendar year. Minsters would have been able to set a permanent cap. The amendment, which was not moved to a vote, was signed by more than 60 MPs.Creasy told the Commons: "Obscene wealth is increasingly dictating who is heard, whether we like it or not, what issues are being prioritised and whose interests shape policy decisions."The Walthamstow MP added that there was a "need to act now to protect the next general election". Her proposals would have exempted trade unions from the donation cap, with the MP saying this is "already well regulated" and "clean money".Kruger highlighted the millions of pounds donated by trade unions to the Labour Party as he criticised the proposals and the bill.The MP for East Wiltshire said: "The claim is made that this bill will defend democracy, but actually it's a flagrantly partisan attempt to kneecap Reform UK."The former Conservative MP added: "The suggestion is made that this bill will restore trust in politics and that is exactly what is needed."But what they all mean is to restore trust in the class of politicians and in the political parties that have got us into the mess that we are in, including the party I'm afraid to say I was part of which is why I left it. We need change."Responding for the government, Eshalomi said the bill "already contains a package of significant measures designed to strengthen the political finance regime whilst ensuring that legitimate donors can continue to fund election campaigns".The communities minister added that the prime minister was among those "determined to tackle the UK-based issue of mega-donors in UK politics"."That is why I'm happy to commit and announce the new cross-government task and finish team will be working at pace to find a solution without unintended consequences," Eshalomi said.  "I can reassure members that once these solutions have been found, we would want them in force as soon as possible."Full details of the new team's remit have yet to be confirmed by the government.It last month emerged that Burnham registered accepting £345,000 of donations over the past year, including £164,347 from businessman Lord Sainsbury.The Liberal Democrats proposed establishing a royal commission to make recommendations for a cap on political donations and the "effectiveness" of existing campaign expenditure limits.This proposal was rejected in the Commons by 427 votes to 85, majority 342.Green Party MP Ellie Chowns said Creasy had made a "clear case" for a cap on all donations, adding she would prefer it to be lower and suggested £50,000 a year.Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam said it was a "noble aim" to protect UK democracy from foreign influence but changes proposed by the government had not always been produced with "proper care and attention".In March, the government said donations in cryptocurrency to UK political parties would be banned alongside the move to cap donations of British citizens living abroad at £100,000 annually.Ministers later announced overseas voters moving to the UK would be prevented from giving more than £100,000 in political donations for a year after their arrival.This was announced alongside tougher checks on company donations, which they believe will help stop foreign money from influencing UK elections.The bill also contains measures to change the voting system, including extending the right to vote to 16- and 17-year-olds.MPs approved the bill at third reading by 411 votes to 102, majority 309, and it will undergo further scrutiny in the House of Lords at a later date.

schema.headline: Burnham to tackle 'mega-donors' in UK politics, minister says

title: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors unwind in Thailand by shopping and bar-hopping
description: US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyageFigure caption, Watch: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Tha
body: US sailors go shopping before hitting the bars in Thailand after 250-day voyageFigure caption, Watch: Why US troops have a history in this raucous Thai cityByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromPattaya, ThailandFar from hitting the bars and fleshpots of the Thai beach resort of Pattaya, in their first hours onshore most of the nearly 5,000 sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln seemed determined to go shopping.At the Hard Rock Hotel – one of two beachside hotels where they were able to stay off the ship – they hung around clutching their recent purchases. But perhaps, after a record 250 days confined inside a grey steel warship, the normality of a trip to the mall might have been just what they needed. With their military haircuts, moustaches and navy t-shirts, they stood out against the usual Pattaya crowd in its flip-flops and beachwear.Image source, ReutersImage caption, US sailors arrived in Thailand on WednesdayNight, though, is where this resort city comes into its own and puts on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars. Local businesses have been hoping to benefit from the sailors' nine months of unspent salary while at sea - but Pattaya's sex industry has been declared off-limits to the sailors, who have been reminded that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand.Conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, has impacted business in Pattaya, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.But on Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to the sailors, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier. By midnight some of the younger sailors there were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.Image caption, Pattaya is renowned for its racy and neon-lit nightlifeConversation over the pounding music was challenging. One older crew member told us they really needed the break. "The news says we've been at sea for nine months. To be honest I've lost track of time", he said. "It got boring. It's never big enough on board. It's big but it still feels like a boat, especially when you're sharing it with thousands of people." How long would it take them to get home to California? "Too long" he said.Shakeira Fairfax, the mother of 25-year-old crew member Jada Fairfax, told Reuters there had been moments over the past few months when "morale was low". She described the period after hostilities broke out in the Middle East as an "uncertain" and "scary" time."I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'mum', I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," Fairfax added.The crew have been well-drilled not to talk about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its long combat deployment in the operation against Iran, which have been the subject of criticism back in the US. Some sailors were wary of making any conversation at all. Others referred journalists' questions to their media teams. Visible everywhere in Pattaya were the men wearing t-shirts emblazoned with the letters SLG, or Shore Liaison Group. It is their job to maintain discipline on land, to watch out for the crew members, some of whom are very young and inexperienced, and to co-ordinate with the local authorities during port calls.US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson did not answer questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing while in Pattaya, saying that "we're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can".US personnel, he added, would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".Image source, ReutersImage caption, The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier has spent nine months at seaThe decision by the USS Abraham Lincoln to stop in Pattaya makes a lot of sense. Port calls by the US Navy in Thailand, a long-standing treaty ally, are routine with well-established protocols. It is also on the ship's route from the Gulf to California, giving the crew a chance to let off steam, and enjoy a break from the demands of life on board a warship.If their stop in Thailand does the trick, any frustration they may feel over their unexpectedly long and tough mission may have dissipated by the time they get home.

schema.headline: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors unwind in Thailand by shopping and bar-hopping

title: How much should you give to the office whip-round?
description: Stingy bosses and spare change: How much should you give to the office whip-round?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Office collections for coll
body: Stingy bosses and spare change: How much should you give to the office whip-round?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Office collections for colleagues are a tradition but can raise awkward questionsByAlex TaylorBBC News reporterReporting fromLondonLove them, hate them or barely know them, it's a colleague's birthday, wedding or  leaving do and there's a collection to mark the occasion.So how much should you give? And if you're the person organising the collection, how do you chase without feeling like a loan shark or exposing unspoken team dynamics?'It depends if I like you'The politics of the office whip-round are so sensitive that everyone the BBC spoke to asked us not to use their real name.For those on a tight budget, the rule is simple: only give to colleagues you've worked with directly.Lucy, a senior therapist in healthcare, says: "If we haven't worked together, my purse is staying shut."There's a blunter unspoken truth beneath the surface. "It also depends on if I like you," she admits."One colleague's whole demeanor annoyed me, so when she moved roles, I wanted to celebrate with my own drink - not give her money."Former music journalist Layla is similar, only contributing if she "really likes" the person.Yet she often avoids office collections on principle, not personality, disliking how impersonal they can feel."I'd rather buy my own gift for someone I care about. I hate having to be forced to contribute to a joint collection out of some rubbish sense of obligation," she says.The decision to give also comes with a question of how much.Barker has a decade's worth of experience organising and contributing to various collections at a large multi-national company, where he works in research and production.He says it's normally the same half a dozen people that contribute generously, irrespective of the person or the occasion.The average a worker gave to a collection was £11.65 in the first three months of the year, according to analysis of over 5,000 contributions by website GiftRound. Figure caption, We ask workers in London how much they'd give towards a colleague's leaving giftJunior workers can often face the biggest dilemma. Felicity, now mid-career, remembers one horror story from her first job as a teenager.Working at a car garage aged 17, she was suddenly thrust an envelope to give money for a mechanic who was retiring. The team was small and tight-knit, so everyone was expected to contribute."Not only did I not really know anyone at that stage, but I also had no money to give - I was still living at home and being paid hardly anything."As it was after lunch, I'd used my notes. In a panic I threw in all the spare change I had left, basically a load of coppers."She says: "I thought I'd got away with it until the person collecting shouted 'who on earth put in all this change'. Everyone laughed and I couldn't ever admit it was me."Today, Felicity usually gives between £5 and £10 but goes up to £20 for a close work friend or long-time colleague.Office politicsBarker says it tends to be rank-and-file workers who contribute most often."Surprisingly – to me – they're not some of the best paid people in the department," he explains. "Often those in senior positions don't give".Those on big wages not paying their way may seem stingy. But the reality from the top can look very different, as former senior civil service veteran Darren explains.In a leadership position managing over 200 people, many of them contractors, office collections were common as staff churn was frequent.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The politics of the office whip-round can be a sensitive topic Darren found the implicit expectation to give as director became overwhelming."Eventually I found I just couldn't keep up and would be spending hundreds, often on people I didn't know at all," he says.As a middle ground, he decided to sign cards and only give money if he'd had direct contact. This stopped him feeling disingenuous and giving resentfully.But the card-not-cash compromise has become harder as collections move online, with amounts often shown alongside the names of individuals by default.Of course, these days, alongside emails, there's always the ever-present work WhatsApp group.Healthcare worker Jeffrey says he's still reeling from seeing staff donations toward the family of a deceased patient being openly listed in the agency chat, individual donation amounts included.Whether to chase colleaguesShould you chase contributions - and note who's given and who has not?Lucy believes so."I send one email to those who haven't paid, making clear that those who have contributed are not included in the email. You'd be surprised how quickly people reply," she says.She then gets a more junior colleague to send another, final, chaser on her behalf."And yes, I keep a list on paper, too. I don't forget," she adds.Barker doesn't agree with this stance."I don't like to nag," he says. Instead he prefers a single reminder to all that preserves team unity.Pssst... try these expert tips Thomas Roulet, professor of organisational psychology and leadership at Cambridge University, says:Prioritise direct colleagues and close relationships: It's generally socially acceptable to limit giving toward wider team membersDo not chase people individually: And do not chase them collectively more than once. Some may be financially strugglingInclude a card as an alternative: It costs the contributor nothing and feels like a souvenir for the recipientThe gift should be symbolic: Choose a gift for its individual significance rather than monetary value.

schema.headline: How much should you give to the office whip-round?

title: Is sleep tracking making your sleep worse?
description: Chasing a perfect sleep score? You could be making it worse ByBBC NewsSleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of
body: Chasing a perfect sleep score? You could be making it worse ByBBC NewsSleep scores, magnesium, white noise machines - what was once the simple act of sleeping has become a minefield.Trying to optimise sleep in this way is called "sleepmaxxing". Take it too far, and you could end up with "orthosomnia" - the clinical term for an obsession with achieving perfect sleep.While it's not formally recognised as a condition in the UK, doctors tell the BBC they've noticed signs of orthosomnia in their patients, with some bringing their sleep tracker data into appointments convinced, wrongly, that they have a sleep disorder. That fixation with sleep is actually making people's sleep worse, they warn.So how and why did sleep become so complicated? And if sleepmaxxing isn't the answer, what is the elusive secret to a good night's sleep?'Sleep scores are completely made up'The first commercial fitness tracker to incorporate sleep analysis was the Fitbit Classic in 2009. Since then, many others - including Garmin, Whoop and Apple - have integrated sleep trackers into wrist-worn devices, as have smart rings such as Oura, Ultrahuman and RingConn.These devices vary, but in general they all provide users with a report of their night, broken down by sleep stages - time awake, light sleep, deep sleep, and REM (rapid eye movement). Many also give users a "sleep score".But the concept of a sleep score is "completely made up", according to Dr Alanna Hare, consultant of sleep medicine at the Royal Brompton Hospital in London."There's nothing recognised in sleep science that is a 'sleep score'," she tells the BBC. "That's just been created by manufacturers."Figure caption, How sleep-tracking can make your sleep worseHare says she's noticed trackers causing anxiety among her patients."I've noticed more patients coming to me with data from various trackers, with lots of questions about sleep that... is probably contributing to their sleep difficulties," she says.Even though some have had medical tests with reassuring results, this hasn't allayed their fears, she adds."It's great that there's more focus on sleep as part of wellness," she adds. "But sleep just does not respond well to attempts to perfect it."One proposed lawsuit against Oura, filed last month in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to accurately measure sleep quality and sleep stages, and instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have "a coin flip's chance of being correct".In response, Oura told the BBC that it "stand[s] behind our science, research and accuracy claims"."We're committed to clearly communicating what Oura measures, what it estimates, and how members should use that information," the company added. Daytime impactStudies also show sleep trackers can affect how you function during the day, even if they're not accurate.In one study, external from the University of Oxford, participants were given sleep trackers which assigned them a sleep score. The scores were randomised, however, and had no relation to how the participants had actually slept.The next day participants rated their mood, fatigue levels and alertness, before tests checking their focus and reaction times.Researchers found that the people told they'd slept badly reported feeling more fatigued, and were less mentally alert - even though the sleep scores were all fake.'Cycle of worrying'This is something Jess Hill says she noticed in herself after getting a Garmin watch several years ago."I started to rely on the watch as my Bible for whether I slept well or not," the 32-year-old HR professional from London tells the BBC."I would think, 'I've had awful sleep so I'm going to really struggle today', even if I actually probably had okay sleep. If I'd slept really well, I'd be convinced I'd have to be on top - even though I was tired, I was pushing through things."Image source, Jess HillImage caption, Jess Hill was "obsessed" with her Garmin's sleep scores for about three yearsHer "obsession", as she describes it, with getting a high sleep score lasted three years, until earlier this year, when she started to notice the watch wasn't reflecting how she'd actually slept."I was awake the other week for four hours in the night, and my watch was like 'wow, great sleep!' - I literally was awake from 01:00 until 05:00," she says.The BBC has approached Garmin for comment.Image caption, Jess's sleep scores weren't matching how she actually feltDr Neil Stanley, sleep expert and author of the book How to Sleep Well, argues that gamifying sleep is creating more disordered sleeping."The thing with tracking your sleep is that it gives you a number, and this means you have a target," he tells the BBC. "So you get into this cycle of worrying about your quality of sleep or the quantity of sleep based on figures."He says he carried out research into actigraphy - wrist-worn sleep trackers - around 40 years ago. Though commercial trackers now are a bit more sophisticated, they work in much the same way - by measuring your movement - and have the same limitations, he says."If you want to measure sleep, you have to measure the brain," Stanley adds. "Unless you're measuring the brain's activities, you're not measuring sleep."So how can we actually sleep well?Hare recommends:Keeping your bedroom cool, dark and quiet - within reason. "That doesn't mean it needs to be pitch black, exactly 16C or totally silent," she says. "It should be coolish, darkish and quietish."Seeing bright light in the morning, which is good for regulating your circadian rhythm - that is, your body's natural clock.Doing light exercise, and eating a "healthy, Mediterranean-style diet with plenty of plant variability".Above all, keeping it simple - "anything else, you don't need it".

schema.headline: Is sleep tracking making your sleep worse?

title: England v Australia Ashes ticket price increase 'really poor' - Michael Vaughan
description: Former England captain Michael Vaughan has called a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston "really poor".The Birmingh
body: Former England captain Michael Vaughan has called a 43% ticket price increase for next year's men's Ashes Test at Edgbaston "really poor".The Birmingham ground will host the third Test of the best-of-five series between England and Australia next summer with ticket prices in the Hollies Stand - which holds almost 6,000 spectators - costing £165, up from £115 in 2023.Elsewhere in the stadium, members can purchase tickets for £92, but the cheapest adult tickets across the first three days are £115, with every ticket carrying a £2.50 booking fee."This is really poor," Vaughan posted on social media in response to the news.Following the 2023 series, which ended in a 2-2 draw after Australia won the first two Tests (at Edgbaston and Lord's), the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) said "every day sold out in advance, with total attendance topping 545,000".Despite Warwickshire's Edgbaston stadium being at a reduced capacity because of the construction of an on-site hotel, tickets for next week's third Test between England and Pakistan, which range between £57.50-£87.50 for adults, have not sold out.The ticket ballot for the 2027 Ashes opened on Wednesday, with prices more expensive at Lord's and the Oval in London, with the best tickets at £190 and £185.England, who lost 4-1 in Australia last winter, begin their quest to regain the Ashes at Trent Bridge in Nottingham on 18 June.The second Ashes Test at Lord's begins on 30 June and the third at Edgbaston on 8 July.The Utilita Bowl in Southampton will become the 10th UK ground to host a men's Ashes Test when the fourth Test gets under way on 21 July, with the series concluding at the Kia Oval from 29 July.BBC Sport has contacted the ECB and the five Test venues for comment.

schema.headline: England v Australia Ashes ticket price increase 'really poor' - Michael Vaughan

title: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference
description: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in
body: Reform UK begin their annual conference in Birmingham a bigger party than they were a year ago, their numbers swelled at Westminster, at Holyrood, in the Senedd and in local authorities.But they also gather amid significant political headwinds, much of which revolve around money.There was that whopping £5m gift to Nigel Farage from Christopher Harborne, the Thailand based British billionaire, and the long running row about whether the money should have been declared by Farage once he became an MP.Then there is, among other things, the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to the party during the last general election campaign.Reform insists that it "takes pride in its stringent vetting of donations."When the party got together in the same West Midlands venue a year ago, they were an insurgency provoking intrigue and attention and demonstrating plenty of momentum.Indeed that momentum was so significant that it was a major factor, perhaps the major factor, in accelerating the demise of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, because the potential prospect of a Reform government frightened the Labour Party to its core. Would Starmer, its then desperately unpopular leader, help or hinder their attempts to take on Farage? Hinder was the eventually overwhelming view within Labour, and so Starmer was a goner.But politics can change, and change quickly. With Starmer out and Burnham in, there is early evidence of some support for Labour picking up. No longer are Reform comfortably leading in all the opinion polls - in some they're not leading at all. Add to this a more confident and prominent Kemi Badenoch leading the Conservatives and the recent rise too of Restore Britain, the outfit set up by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe. And the Scottish National Party and Plaid Cymru won and so beat them in the devolved elections in Scotland and Wales respectively. In other words, collectively Reform's opponents appear more energised and popular.Make no mistake, no party at a UK wide level is popular at the moment, but the scrap appears more evenly matched than it did.Into that mix, Reform's continued prominence has brought what prominence always brings: scrutiny. Nigel Farage is a candidate for prime minister; his senior team candidates for the great offices of state.When I interviewed Farage at Reform HQ yesterday, on the specifics of the £5m gift and the police investigation he maintained they've acted appropriately.But he offered an insight into how he perceives the hurricane of questions he faces."I think what you're seeing is the establishment - in a very coordinated way - fighting back," he claimed.I suggested he sounded like a conspiracy theorist, implying the whole world was out to get him.His answer was instructive: "When you read in the newspaper you're under investigation, and you don't even know a complaint's been made, you can see the degree of collusion that has gone on between interested parties. This will not stop. They will continually try and do this to us."Who's they? I pressed. He mentioned the House of Commons and House of Lords – full of his political opponents – but didn't name anyone or anything else."I'm talking about normal human behaviour. People who, people who hold positions of power, influence, and money don't want new kids on the block succeeding."Let's be clear – it is a big claim to allege collusion between institutions or organisations collectively seeking to undermine him and his party, and there is no evidence for it.But, crucially, you hear in his answer a sense of why he perceives that - that is what it feels like.The question, as Reform's conference gets under way, is how the party approaches the coming days and the coming months.Will Nigel Farage ditch the "aggrieved" tone he has been accused of adopting recently?

schema.headline: Chris Mason: Reform face headwinds as they gather for conference

title: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig
description: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig mark
body: The heads of Nato and the European Commission have warned Russia is growing increasingly reckless and vowed to respond to a "new normal"."Leipzig marks a new escalation on European Union soil directly attributed to Russia," said Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a day after Germany blamed Russia for a failed drone attack on Leipzig airport.Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance, which includes the US, stood "in full solidarity with Germany".Russia rejects accusations it targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane on 4 August with an explosives-laden drone. It has responded to new German sanctions by saying it will close Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centres in Russia.The drone was defused by a robot at Leipzig/Halle airport and a second drone is thought to have collided with another cargo plane.A third drone was reportedly found 10 days later at the airport, which is an important Nato hub and is regularly used by Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft.It was not until Tuesday that the German government said police investigations and intelligence finding had proved that Russia was behind the incidents. The interior minister said that the drone's configuration, components, explosives and detonator were all known from other Russian hybrid operations.Two suspects have reportedly been identified in the Leipzig attack, including a Belarusian with a Russian passport who entered on a tourist visa, and another with Latvian and Russian passports who arrived by plane in Berlin and flew out two days before the failed attack.Berlin has said it will close the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as the Russian House cultural institution, widely suspected in Berlin of acting as a propaganda outlet for the Kremlin.The Russian foreign ministry said Berlin had offered no evidence to back its claims. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov announced that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centres in Moscow, St Petersburg and Yekaterinburg would close in response to Berlin's actions.Earlier, Germany's chargé d'affaires Bernd Finke was summoned to hear Moscow's rejection of Berlin's "entirely unfounded accusations".Russian President Vladimir Putin has condemned Germany's measures as a serious mistake that "clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people".Asked whether Moscow would be prepared to sever relations with Berlin, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Grushko answered "maybe", but said for now it was giving diplomacy a chance.Critics in Germany suggested the German response was relatively weak, but Berlin has its eye on a more co-ordinated response with its allies, including extended EU sanctions and entry restrictions on Russian visitors across the bloc.Von der Leyen was clear in her statement that the Leipzig attack had involved "military-grade material carried out by Russian operatives on European Union soil"."We will not tolerate it," she said. "We have to step up and that means being ready to respond to Russia's recklessness faster and better."While she was meeting Rutte in Brussels, EU foreign ministers had gathered at Wicklow in Ireland, where France's Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said action could be taken on a European level against Russia's so-called "shadow fleet" of ships carrying oil and other cargo aimed at avoiding EU sanctions.Barrot and fellow ministers from Belgium and the Netherlands said they had summoned Russian ambassadors in protest at the attack.Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said it was obvious that Russia saw no political cost in its hybrid operations against European allies.EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said they were working on how to tighten enforcement of existing sanctions, and added there was broad support for an EU visa entry ban on Russian ex-combatants as well as stricter visa limits on Russian tourists.Several EU countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Poland and Spain, are pushing for more than €193bn (£165bn) in frozen Russian assets to be used to help Ukraine. The idea was first planned at the end of 2025, and rejected by Belgium where the money is held. However, Belgium's position is unchanged because it fears being held financially liable by the courts.The Leipzig attack was part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents, including drones and interference with critical infrastructure, von der Leyen said.Mark Rutte added there had been increased risk to Europeans from drones and missiles crossing into countries on the Alliance's eastern flank, and there had been more "malign activities targeting our territory directly, whether it is fires set in factories producing defence equipment for Ukraine or indeed the Russian hybrid attack in Leipzig".Several acts of suspected sabotage have been reported in Germany in the past 24 hours alone, including two attacks on electricity substations, one in the east and one in the west near Cologne.Although authorities do not yet know who was behind the incidents, North Rhine-Westphalia Interior Minister Herbert Reul said an attack that targeted power lines at Bergheim in western Germany was deliberate and whoever had carried out was attacking the country as a whole."We are investigating two possibilities: sabotage directed by a foreign state and left-wing extremism," he said.Several power lines failed prompting five power plant units to go offline at two separate coal-fired power stations. Police said six launching devices had been found in a field.High-voltage power lines were damaged near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant in Brandenburg early on Tuesday and explosive devices were later found at a substation.Meanwhile, in neighbouring Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a fire at a factory producing combat drones at Skarżysko-Kamienna, 140km (85 miles) south of Warsaw was a deliberate act of arson and sabotage. Arson has also not been ruled out in a fire at a factory in Lublin on Sunday night.Von der Leyen said sanctions had already been used to deter Russia, and EU foreign ministers were discussing further ways of "cutting deeper in Russia's war chest".The EU has already agreed to loan Ukraine €90bn (£77bn), and von der Leyen said Kyiv had asked for billions of extra euros in funding to help pay for PAC-3 air defence missiles. Work was already taking place on a joint Europe-Ukraine Freyja anti-ballistic missile defence project, she added.She promised that Europe and Nato would just maintain pressure on Moscow but "we will increase it and we will not stop, not until Russia stops bombing and killing innocent men, women and children in Ukraine".

schema.headline: EU and Nato vow to step up pressure on Russia after 'new escalation' in Leipzig

title: B&Q and Five Guys among firms which paid staff below minimum wage
description: DIY store B&Q and the fast food chain Five Guys are among hundreds of UK businesses named by the government for paying staff below the minimum wage.Mo
body: DIY store B&Q and the fast food chain Five Guys are among hundreds of UK businesses named by the government for paying staff below the minimum wage.More than 600 employers were ordered to pay affected workers the outstanding wages, with £4m returned to workers, according to the Department for Business and Trade.The firms have also been issued penalties worth £7m.B&Q said the underpayments were unintentional and the result of calculations involving geographical allowances, while Five Guys blamed "technical differences in how payroll regulations were applied".The list of 658 businesses includes shops, restaurants, nurseries, social care providers and a handful of NHS trusts. The government did not say over what time period the underpayments spanned.Minimum wage is £12.71 for staff aged 21 and over. For 18 to 20 year olds the rate is £10.85, and for under 18s and apprentices it is £8.B&Q underpaid 4,530 workers a total of more than £456,000, according to the government.B&Q said in response: "The shortfalls in payments were unintentional. They relate to calculations involving geographical allowances which are paid in addition to minimum hourly rates. All affected colleagues were quickly paid in full in July 2025."Five Guys, named in the list as owing over £54,000 to 3,699 staff, said "technical differences in how payroll regulations were applied" led to its underpayments, which were identified in a review by the HMRC, the UK's revenue and tax authority."We worked closely and transparently with HMRC throughout the process and have made all required payments to affected current and former employees," the company said.St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group failed to pay over £123,000 to 75 workers, according to the list, which also says St George's University Hospitals in Wandsworth, London, underpaid 55 workers.A spokesman for the two hospital trusts said that "no colleagues were underpaid"."This relates to a technical compliance issue where part of their salary for a non tax-deductable 'salary sacrifice' (for example, towards childcare) was not counted towards the national minimum wage, even though their gross salary was above the national minimum wage," he said.A spokesperson said apprentices at Norfolk Community Health and Care NHS Trust were inadvertently underpaid between 2019 and 2023.They said while their pay met the requirements for their contracted hours, meetings, handovers and time spent changing into uniform hadn't been accounted for, adding the trust has since changed policies and practices.The other trust named has been contacted for comment.There were also several nursing homes on the list, and multiple childcare providers.Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said the government was determined to stamp out the practice of "short-changing your staff"."The best businesses know that looking after your workers isn't just the right thing to do, it's the smart thing to do," he said.Kate Dearden, minister for the future of work, said: "Underpaying your staff is illegal, and we will not let workers foot the bill for their boss failing to follow the rules.""Every employer should check their payroll now and reach out to Acas if they need further support," she added.The first 10 employers on the government's list, which was sorted by the amount of wages not paid, are:1.  B&Q Ltd, failed to pay £456,934.72 to 4,530 workers.2.  Elysium Healthcare Holdings 3 Ltd, Borehamwood, failed to pay £330,048.81 to 1,095 workers.3.  St George's, Epsom and St Helier Hospital Group, failed to pay £123,331.97 to 75 workers.4.  Support Staff Services Limited, Slough, failed to pay £119,715.13 to 323 workers.5.  Forest Holidays Ltd, Moira, failed to pay £100,308.68 to 598 workers.6.  St George's University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, London (Wandsworth), failed to pay £77,498.91 to 55 workers.7.  Lanes Group Limited, Leeds, failed to pay £67,893.34 to 297 workers.8.  UK Care Team Ltd, Leicester, LE19, failed to pay £67,082.76 to 99 workers.9.  Five Guys JV Limited, London (Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea), failed to pay £54,642.47 to 3,699 workers.10.  Merlin Cinemas Limited, Redruth, failed to pay £50,198.75 to 181 workers.The list marks the first "naming round" since the Fair Work Agency was set up in April under the Employment Rights Act.As well as enforcing the minimum wage, the agency also will soon tackle practices of denying workers holiday and sick pay.Chair of the agency's advisory board, Matthew Taylor, said naming employers which underpay staff was an important reminder that "paying the minimum wage is not optional - it is the law".He said: "Most employers want to do the right thing, and we will support them to comply, but those who fall short should expect robust enforcement to protect workers and maintain a fair playing field for responsible businesses."

schema.headline: B&Q and Five Guys among firms which paid staff below minimum wage

title: Newspaper headlines: 'City warns Burnham' and 'One in the eye for Andy'
description: Many of the papers reflect on Andy Burnham's first Prime Minister's Questions. The Guardian says he used it to try to calm the bond markets, external
body: Many of the papers reflect on Andy Burnham's first Prime Minister's Questions. The Guardian says he used it to try to calm the bond markets, external ahead of his first budget - with the i Paper warning that he might need to raise £15bn in taxes to fund high borrowing costs, external. The Times highlights the warning from the Labour chairman of the Commons Defence Committee that "vibes alone", external will not be enough to defend the UK. The Daily Mail and the Daily Telegraph say the Conservatives have pledged to reach that target by slashing welfare., externalThe Daily Express is more interested in another potential area of savings, external, reporting that the prime minister's ally, Lord O'Neill, has joined what it calls "hysterical" calls to drop the pension triple lock. It reports that voters would "punish" the prime minister for such a move.The Sun says that an extra "surge" of French police - to tackle small boat crossings - will consist of what it calls just 45 "do-nothing" officers., external It draws on images from the Bayeux Tapestry to illustrate the story and urges the Prime Minister to "prevent a stitch-up" by the French. Recalling King Harold's fate, it describes Macron's promise as "one in the eye for Andy".The Daily Mail reports criticism from the Conservatives of what the party calls a "massive new quango" to reform the civil service., external It quotes the First Secretary of State Louise Haigh as saying the government needs to "tear away red tape". The paper's cartoonist pictures one MP telling another: "We've commissioned a quango to reduce our quangos."The Guardian says the Green party leader in England and Wales, Zack Polanski, has moved a step closer to becoming an MP, external.  It says party members in the seat vacated by Sir Keir Starmer are supporting him to become their candidate to replace him. But the Times reports his hopes could be "scuppered, external by his own party members who may prefer a Palestinian candidate or a pro-Gaza independent".

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'City warns Burnham' and 'One in the eye for Andy'

title: El Niño 'supersized' as countries race to prepare for extreme weather, UN warns
description: Image source, Florian Plaucheur/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, El Niño brought intense flooding and landslides to southern Brazil in 2024ByEsme St
body: Image source, Florian Plaucheur/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, El Niño brought intense flooding and landslides to southern Brazil in 2024ByEsme Stallardsenior climate and science reporterMark Poynting and Becky DaleBBC Verify and Yvette Tan, Tiffanie Turnbull and Nikita YadavThe world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned.The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027.El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding.Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change."El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said.The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups.The WMO - a UN agency -  said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible.WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world."El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere.Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño.In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event.But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest.This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin.Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average.Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast.With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia.It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change. El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC.This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover."[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed," said Hobday.Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions.Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring.But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried.Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruptionWhile the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months.Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires.On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall.About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year.Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year.A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month"."The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy.Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land.Image source, Monirul Bhuiyan/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Countries in Southern Africa, like Botswana, experienced severe drought during the last El Niño eventStronger typhoons and landslide riskThousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño.In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead.And in August, more than 1m people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds.Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding."We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO.This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain.Peru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific.Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away.Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm."He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts.At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak.However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.Get in touchWhat questions or concerns do you have about El Niño?

schema.headline: El Niño 'supersized' as countries race to prepare for extreme weather, UN warns

title: South Africa's Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice and compensation
description: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville ByPumza FihlaniReporting fromSharpevilleAbraham Mofokeng still
body: Image caption, Abraham Mofokeng was 20 when he joined a peaceful protest in Sharpeville ByPumza FihlaniReporting fromSharpevilleAbraham Mofokeng still carries the wounds of the bloody suppression of a protest in South Africa 66 years ago. In what became known as the Sharpeville massacre, police infamously opened fire on thousands of peaceful demonstrators.A bullet is still lodged in Mofokeng's spine, and he has a gentle limp from a gunshot to the leg."We weren't seen as people," the 86-year-old tells the BBC as he explains the reasons he joined the demonstration on 21 March 1960 against the repressive laws of the white-minority government."All you were good for was working. You couldn't question them, you were supposed to just do as you're told."The massacre at Sharpeville, which he survived, exposed to the world the violence of the racist apartheid system - yet thanks to an indemnity law passed a year after the killings, none of the perpetrators were ever prosecuted.Mofokeng is now part of a legal case set to be announced on Thursday that will seek to overturn this law.At least 69 protesters were shot dead by police on that day in 1960, becoming a pivotal event in the history of the anti-apartheid movement.Though Sharpeville may be a place name rich in historical resonance, it scarcely looks like a site that symbolises the struggle: the township is slowly crumbling. The once tarred roads of this area south of Johannesburg are returning to dirt. Many of the houses are still the small, brown-faced brick homes built under the apartheid-era government. The earth is dry and barren - heaps of rubbish are piling up throughout the neighbourhood.While the legalised system of racism was buried in 1994 when the country held its first democratic election and elected Nelson Mandela as president, its scars remain.There have been attempts at redress - not least through the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC) - set up by Mandela's government to investigate crimes committed during the apartheid era.But the Sharpeville survivors feel they have not seen justice.Image source, Universal History Archive/UIG via Getty imagesImage caption, Protesters started fleeing as the police opened fireSharpeville's local memorial park, the Human Rights Precinct, tells the story of how the streets of township became the scene of a bloodbath.Inside the park stand 69 white pillars, one for each life lost.The victims were killed while demonstrating against the racist pass laws.At the time, black people were forced to carry a document known as a passbook, known as "dompas" in Afrikaans, which restricted their freedom to move around the country.A person could be beaten and jailed if found without it - or if found in a "whites-only" area without permission.Many heeded the call from the leaders of the Pan Africanist Congress in March 1960 to march in protest against the dompas, including then-20-year-old Mofokeng."The life we were living under apartheid was a life of oppression. We could not move around freely. We ended up planning to march to the police station against these passbooks that were being used to oppress us," he says.Thousands turned up to what they thought would be a peaceful protest."[The police] had rifles, machetes, even shields. We explained to the police that we didn't want the passes anymore and we were prepared to go to prison. There was a commotion, then all hell broke loose when the police started shooting."Mofokeng was among the more than 200 people injured and recent estimates by South African researchers have revised upwards the number who died to as many as 91.Image caption, Larazus Magotsi witnessed police shooting at some who were trying to get up from the groundAnother survivor, Larazus Magotsi - now 90 - walks along the long row of graves in the cemetery where most of those who died are buried. Among them is a headstone marking where a 12-year-old was laid to rest.Magotsi's eyes are filled with tears as he struggles to compose himself."We heard gunshots and ran and hid inside a store, peeping to see what was happening outside," he says."People were lying on the ground. When we looked out again, we saw that some were trying to get up, but the police were just shooting at them."Others were using machetes to strike the heads of people who were still moving."It is thought that more than 1,300 bullets were shot into the crowd. Archive photos show policemen walking among the corpses, lying where they fell, in the immediate aftermath of the massacre.The only legal case that followed the killings was a failed attempt to charge the protesters with affray.Now, survivors and relatives of those who were killed are hoping to overturn the law they say prevents them from getting justice.Image source, Universal History Archive/UIG via Getty imagesImage caption, The photographer Ian Berry later told the BBC that it seemed the man in the centre of this picture was holding his jacket up "as though to protect himself from the bullets"The 1961 Indemnity Act was passed by the apartheid government in the wake of the massacre and protected the police and government from having criminal charges or even civil claims brought against them in relation to what happened at Sharpeville.Despite more than 30 years of democratic rule, that law remains on the statute books.But now South African non-governmental organisation Lawyers for Human Rights, together with UK-based law firm Leigh Day, has filed a case at the High Court arguing that the law is unconstitutional under the new constitution that came into effect in 1994."Apart from the individual damages, what the community's looking for is basically reparations to enable their healing. They feel as though Sharpeville is a forgotten community," says Charne Tracey, one of the lawyers on the case.Part of their court application includes getting a class action certified - if approved this would mean that for the first time dozens of victims and relatives of those killed could collectively sue the state. It could also possibly lead to criminal charges being brought against the alleged perpetrators, if any are still alive."Nothing has been done that assists with their healing and improvement of their quality of life, or remedy the long-term effects of what they've suffered," Tracey says, adding that 70 people could be involved in the class action.Constitutional law expert Prof Frans Viljoen believes having the old law repealed is important because it would help to "clean up" the legislation and "close a chapter on the past"."Although South Africa has a very transformative constitution… The principle of continuity of statehood still applies, which is why the case can be brought against the current state," says Viljoen."So if there were laws in our statute book in 1994, the constitution explicitly says they remain in force until parliament repeals them, abolishes them or changes them," he adds.But he backs attempts to declare the Indemnity Act unconstitutional "to cleanse us of that past".Image caption, Many of those who died in the massacre are buried in a long row in a cemetery in SharpevilleThe TRC, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, was generally praised for bringing together victims and perpetrators who were granted amnesty as long as they, among other conditions, fully disclosed what they had done.But the greatest criticism of the process was that it did not bring about justice for some as people were not jailed for their acts and no police officers applied for amnesty for the Sharpeville shootings.The government told the BBC it had supported apartheid victims over the years, and would continue to do so, but did not oppose survivors and families pursuing legal remedies.When it comes to reparations the justice department said 560 TRC-recognised victims of apartheid-era violence had received individual grants amounting to some $31m (£23m) and though not all Sharpeville survivors and relatives had been identified it encouraged them to come forward.For many in the community of Sharpeville, there is hope that restitution will help heal decades of lingering trauma."Apartheid is dead and buried. A win would bring complete healing, not just for us, but for future generations as well," says Mofokeng."Considering how people died, many have not completely healed."

schema.headline: South Africa's Sharpeville massacre survivors start legal fight for justice and compensation

title: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka continues title defence with one of the quickest Grand Slam wins of her career
description: Sabalenka knows she must the lift the trophy in New York again to stand any chance of preventing Elena Rybakina taking her position at the top of the
body: Sabalenka knows she must the lift the trophy in New York again to stand any chance of preventing Elena Rybakina taking her position at the top of the rankings.Even if Sabalenka does retain the title, Rybakina would still rise to the summit by reaching the semi-finals.Sabalenka losing the top spot seemed unthinkable after a storming start to the season, reaching the Australian Open final and winning the Indian Wells and Miami titles back-to-back.Losing to Rybakina in Melbourne was Sabalenka's only defeat in her first 27 matches of 2026. After completing the Sunshine Double, her win-loss record  leading into the US Open dropped to 17-7 and she has only reached one WTA semi-final in the past five months.Before the final Grand Slam of the season, Sabalenka admitted she had been "dealing with several things" in a period which she knows was far below her best.And, after beating Iatcenko, Sabalenka took umbrage with what she perceived to be a suggestion from a reporter that she had been attending "lots of parties" in the build-up to the US Open."What kind of question is that? Just because I posted some activities with brands, you think that I've been partying [and] not training?" countered Sabalenka.Asked if she was "getting serious" now the tournament was under way, she said: "Oh yeah, I wasn't serious before that. Next question."Sabalenka's pace and power was too much for world number 160 Iatcenko, who managed just three winners compared to the 24 put away by the top seed. Iatcenko looked a bundle of nerves in the biggest match of her career, but composed herself to get on the scoreboard for 5-1 and immediately broke out into a relieved smile.It was merely respite as Sabalenka held to love in fewer than 90 seconds to clinch the opening set.Despite only being on court for 24 minutes, Iatchenko decided she wanted a bathroom break to change her kit - but more likely for a mental reset than anything else.Sabalenka kept loose while she waited by practising her serves and maintained her rhythm as she surged a double break ahead for 3-0 in the second set.It was not all plain-sailing for Sabalenka as she lost serve in a sloppy fourth game, but reasserted her authority with two more breaks as Iatchenko was taught a harsh lesson. The Russian can console herself with the knowledge she has gained valuable experience against the world number one on the biggest court on the planet - and a bumper paycheck.Coming into the US Open, she had earned $300,000 (£220,000) in her career but takes another $190,000 home from New York to reinvest into her future.Earlier on Wednesday, third seed Pegula continued her quest for a maiden Grand Slam singles title with a comfortable victory over fellow American Sofia Kenin.Pegula also has a shot of replacing Sabalenka as world number one if she wins the title, as does fourth seed Coco Gauff, and kept her dream alive with a 6-3 6-1 win.There were also straight-set wins for Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova, SW19 runner-up Karolina Muchova, two-time major semi-finalist Marta Kostyuk and teenage American sensation Iva Jovic as the pattern of few shocks in the women's draw over the opening two rounds continued.

schema.headline: US Open 2026 results: Aryna Sabalenka continues title defence with one of the quickest Grand Slam wins of her career

title: King Charles, Macron and Burnham arrive to view Bayeux Tapestry at British Museum
description: There was also some cross-Channel teasing about the outcome of the Norman invasion story, if not accusations of a stitch up.President Macron commented
body: There was also some cross-Channel teasing about the outcome of the Norman invasion story, if not accusations of a stitch up.President Macron commented at the finish of the tapestry on the "happy end, we're here", while Andy Burnham said: "Made in England, they couldn't bear to show the end… too difficult."The King, speaking inside the Great Court of the British Museum, said the opponents depicted in the tapestry - Normans and Anglo-Saxons - would have been delighted to see this togetherness between France and the UK - "two great nations, which share such fundamental values"."The tapestry's story is one of ambition and uncertainty, of oaths and journeys, of ships, councils, kings, comets and consequences," said the King."Yet it is not merely an English story, nor only a Norman one. Indeed, from the moment of its creation, it may have brought together our two peoples," he said, weaving in the historic importance of the artwork.Burnham joked about his own new role as prime minister - saying the tapestry "showed a new leader emerging from a northern territory and travelling to the south of England".Describing the tapestry as a "masterpiece", President Macron said a loan had first been proposed in the 1930s, but he was delighted that the idea had come to fruition.He spoke of the exhibition in London as an example of how "we are united" and a "reminder of what our countries can do if they join forces", addressing an audience including historian Dame Mary Beard and former prime minister Theresa May.The 70m (230ft) tapestry, originally embroidered in England but kept for centuries in France, tells the story of the Norman Conquest and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.The King and Queen, Macron and his wife Brigitte, and Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel were given the chance to see the historic embroidery in the atmospheric darkness of the British Museum.It's displayed in a long glass illuminated cabinet, with the figures remarkably vivid for something almost a 1,000 years old, and visitors file along, following the story of the Norman invasion.The royal visitors had a close look at key scenes in the tapestry, including the Coronation of King Harold and his death in battle.It's filled with details of medieval life and the King commented on Normans pulling a cart with "an enormous amount of wine".Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said the final scene, showing King Harold with an arrow in his eye, was what she found the most dramatic."We've just been talking to all the schoolchildren, and that's the bit that they really liked and really registered with them," she said."And it's amazing actually that a tapestry that is 1,000 years old can still inspire people to feel such emotion and capture such drama after all this time."Nandy said she was inspired by the way this epic depiction of conflict had "come to symbolise probably the biggest act of friendship on behalf of the French nation".Sending the tapestry to the British Museum was announced by Macron during a state visit to the UK in July 2025, as an emblem of the strong partnership between the countries.There had been fears that moving the fragile tapestry could risk causing damage, but French government sources said display conditions at the British Museum were "ideal".The French authorities welcomed the way that visitors in London would see the tapestry lying flat, rather than upright, with this believed to be better for the conservation of the fibres.It also allows viewers to get a clearer view of all the animals, plants and often bawdy images sewn around the margins of the main narrative.It is believed the final scenes of the tapestry have been lost or destroyed, as it has not always had such careful owners. In the 18th Century, during the French Revolution, it was rescued from being cut up to make covers for soldiers' carts.The Bayeux Tapestry records a much earlier chapter in Anglo-French relations, when King William of Normandy fought King Harold for the throne of England.Using dyed wool stitched onto linen, it shows the competing claims to the throne, the Normans sailing across the Channel and the decisive Battle of Hastings, in which Harold was killed, allowing William the Conqueror to become monarch.The tapestry, believed to have been embroidered by English women for the new Norman rulers in the 1070s, includes 58 separate scenes, with 627 human figures, 737 animals, 37 ships and 23 trees, with a Latin narration accompanying the images.As part of this cultural diplomatic exchange, the UK is lending France one of the British Museum's prize exhibits - treasures from the Anglo-Saxon Sutton Hoo burial.There was strong demand for tickets to see the tapestry, with the exhibition already sold out until the end of 2026.The next tickets, covering visits between January and March 2027, will be available from the British Museum from 21 October.

schema.headline: King Charles, Macron and Burnham arrive to view Bayeux Tapestry at British Museum
